analysis.one_liner: Requires police to get a judge's warrant before using cell-phone tracking devices known as Stingrays.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat with four House committees until the Congress ended, leaving police free to use cell-site simulators without a warrant.
analysis.plain_summary: Cell-site simulators — commonly known as Stingrays — are devices that masquerade as cell towers to locate phones and sweep up information about every nearby device, including bystanders. The bill would make it illegal to use one in the United States without a warrant from a judge, with narrow exceptions for emergencies, foreign intelligence under existing law, and a few specialized uses like prison contraband searches. It would also require notice to people whose phones were swept up, limits on keeping data about bystanders, a civil fine for violations, and a private right to sue. It was introduced with support from one Democrat and one Republican and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who carries a cell phone. Today, police can use a Stingray without a judge's approval, and the device collects location and identity information about every phone in the area, not just the suspect's. The bill would require a warrant showing other methods were tried first, limit how long and how widely the device is used, require disclosure of disruptions to 911 calls, mandate notice to people whose devices were swept up, and let victims sue for up to $500 per violation.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for any individual or entity to knowingly use a cell-site simulator in the United States except under a warrant or a narrow emergency exception, with a fine of up to $250,000 for violations [S2] [S3].

Requires a warrant applicant to show other investigative methods failed or are too dangerous, specify the device's area of effect, certify the narrowest possible use, and disclose any disruption to 911 calls, the suicide crisis hotline, and poison control [S3].

Bars information gathered unlawfully with a simulator, and evidence derived from it, from use in any court or official proceeding, and requires notice to people named in a warrant about whether their device was tracked or intercepted [S3].

Requires the Attorney General to adopt and publish procedures minimizing collection and retention of information about people who are not targets, and gives victims a private right of action with statutory damages up to $500 per violation and attorney fees [S3].

Requires annual unclassified Inspector General reports to Congress on simulator use, including how many devices were swept up that were not targets, to create public oversight of a practice that has largely operated in secret [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies and intelligence agencies, which would lose the ability to use Stingrays on their own authority and would face new warrant, notice, and record-keeping requirements. Manufacturers of the devices would face third-party testing and FCC rulemaking. Police departments acknowledge some urgent investigations could face added delay, which the bill addresses with 48-hour emergency exceptions requiring later judicial approval.

drawbacks.text: The warrant process would add time and paperwork to investigations where police currently use the devices on their own authority; the bill tries to manage this with a 48-hour emergency window but genuine delays in fast-moving cases remain possible [S3].

The bill carves out a number of exceptions — Secret Service protective duties, prison contraband interdiction, equipment testing, and training — and delays full effect for two to three years for devices already in use, so parts of current practice would continue unregulated for years [S3].

Opponents of warrant requirements for location tracking have generally argued it hampers investigations; no organized opposition appears in the record here, and the bill drew only two cosponsors, suggesting little appetite in either chamber.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and broad: a warrant requirement, notice, and a right to sue for a surveillance practice that currently sweeps in bystanders without judicial approval. The costs fall on law enforcement in added process, and the bill takes care to preserve emergency use, foreign intelligence channels, and prison security. The main weakness is not the design but the delay — two to three years before existing devices are covered — and the carve-outs. On balance the protections outweigh the compliance burden, and the bill's death means the status quo of warrantless use continues.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to four House committees on the day it was introduced, one of them passed it to a subcommittee, and no committee ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Lieu introduced the Cell-Site Simulator Warrant Act of 2021 with Rep. Tom McClintock as an original cosponsor, giving it one Democratic and one Republican sponsor [S3] [S4].
On introduction it was referred to the House Judiciary, Intelligence, Energy and Commerce, and Armed Services Committees [S5].
The only further action was referral to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Communications and Technology the next day [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 with the bill still in committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies and the intelligence community keep their current ability to use cell-site simulators without a warrant, and device manufacturers keep selling into an unregulated market. Cell phone users gain nothing; the warrantless practice the bill targeted continues.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Law enforcement and surveillance device makers

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by one Democrat and one Republican and opposed by no recorded vote; its failure reflected committee inaction across both sides, not a partisan fight.

industries.note: The bill would end their ability to use Stingrays without a judge's warrant and require notice, minimization of bystander data, and annual public reporting. Their institutional interest in warrantless tracking runs against the public's interest in privacy and due process. Note the bill died, so agencies lost nothing.

The devices' market exists because agencies buy them for tracking; the bill would require FCC-accredited third-party testing of each model and compliance with FCC rules, adding cost, while leaving a legal market intact under warrant. Their interest in unrestricted sales runs against bystanders' privacy.
Every warrant application would require certification that the specific device model passed third-party inspection, creating paid testing work. Their gain comes from a check that protects the public.
